strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful idea: adapting byte-pair-style motif tokenization to quantized time series, yielding variable-length tokens that can reduce autoregressive sequence length. The method is simple, broadly applicable to discrete-vocabulary forecasters, and well motivated by the inefficiency of per-sample tokenization.

The empirical section is substantial in scale: the authors train multiple T5/Chronos-style models, study three compression regimes, compare against Chronos, MOMENT, Morai, and several supervised forecasting baselines, and include ablations over quantization granularity, minimum motif frequency, training data size, preprocessing choices, and conditional decoding.

Conditional decoding is an elegant lightweight calibration/dequantization mechanism. The analytic solution is straightforward, cheap, and the reported gains are consistent across many settings, especially for coarser tokenizers.
The paper is generally well organized and readable, with helpful pseudocode and a frank note that no large hyperparameter search was performed due to training cost.
weaknesses: The central performance comparison is not fully controlled. The proposed tokenizer uses 128 compressed tokens as context, which can correspond to far more raw time steps than Chronos' 128 per-sample tokens and more than the 384-sample context used for patch baselines. Thus part of the forecasting gain may come from giving the model substantially longer raw history, not solely from a better tokenization inductive bias.

The efficiency claims are somewhat overstated. Reported acceleration is obtained by selecting the fastest proposed model that still beats the best Chronos reference, mixing model size, tokenizer choice, and accuracy thresholds. This is useful practically, but it is not a clean same-model or same-accuracy efficiency comparison, and one dataset even shows poor speedup for the best-MSE setting.

Conditional decoding is presented as a universal post-hoc improvement, but the main model-dependent experiment fits it on the train split of each evaluation dataset. This is closer to target-domain calibration than pure zero-shot deployment, and the paper should separate zero-shot, calibrated, and supervised-use cases more explicitly.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript gives high-level hyperparameters, pseudocode, dataset choices, and compute estimates, but does not appear to commit to releasing the trained tokenizers/models/code. Reproducing the full study also requires thousands of H100 GPU hours, making small implementation ambiguities consequential.

The evaluation is narrower than the claims suggest: only five benchmark datasets, a single 64-step horizon in the main comparison, MSE as the dominant metric, and apparently single test runs without confidence intervals or seed variability. Time-series foundation models are often assessed over more datasets, horizons, and probabilistic metrics.

Some methodological details need clarification for soundness, especially normalization/scaling. The paper says each series is normalized to zero mean and unit standard deviation; for forecasting this must be computed only from the observed context to avoid future leakage, but the manuscript does not make this explicit.

Comparisons to MOMENT, Morai, and supervised baselines are informative but not decisive because the models differ in architecture, training data, objective, context length, and forecast horizon. The authors acknowledge some of this, but the text still uses these comparisons to support broad superiority claims.

The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal. The environmental benefit claim is plausible from compression, but the paper also reports very large training compute and does not quantify net cost, release risks, or applicability limits for safety-critical forecasting domains.

strengths: The core idea of applying BPE-style motif tokenization to discretized time series is intuitive, technically plausible, and potentially useful for reducing autoregressive sequence length in time-series foundation models.

The paper includes several ablations over quantization granularity, minimum motif occurrence, tokenizer training set size, and compression, which helps illuminate some tradeoffs of the proposed tokenizer.
The presentation is generally clear, with understandable figures and pseudocode for vocabulary construction and tokenization.
The work makes a reasonable attempt to compare against sample-wise Chronos-style tokenization and patch-based foundation models, and the reported gains are sometimes large.
weaknesses: The empirical protocol substantially weakens the central claims. Conditional decoding is trained on the train split of each evaluation dataset and then reported alongside zero-shot results, so the strongest performance numbers are not truly zero-shot. This is especially problematic because the abstract and main tables emphasize large MSE reductions from conditional decoding.

Model and tokenizer selection appear to be based on best test-set MSE across multiple tokenizers and model sizes, without a clearly separated validation protocol. This risks test-set overfitting and makes the headline improvements difficult to interpret.

Efficiency claims are overstated. The paper often reports compression or cherry-picked acceleration points rather than a systematic wall-clock, memory, throughput, and quality tradeoff. Some reported acceleration entries are even below 1x, and comparisons across model sizes conflate tokenizer efficiency with choosing a smaller model.

Comparisons to patch-based methods such as MOMENT and Morai are not controlled because architectures, training data, objectives, and context lengths differ. The paper acknowledges this, but still uses these results to support broad claims about superiority over patching.

Evaluation scope is narrow for an ICML-level foundation-model claim: only five datasets, a single short forecasting horizon of 64 samples in the main experiments, mostly univariate framing, and no convincing analysis of robustness across horizons, frequencies, multivariate settings, or distribution shifts.

The paper reports single test evaluations with no uncertainty estimates, seeds, or significance analysis. Given the many trained models and configuration choices, this makes the evidence less reliable.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript gives some computational cost estimates, but does not provide enough detail on training hyperparameters, data preprocessing, model selection, seeds, or code/artifact availability to allow others to reliably reproduce the main claims, and the stated cost of thousands of H100 hours is prohibitive.

The limitations section is too thin. It mentions lack of hyperparameter search and newer architectures, but does not adequately discuss the non-zero-shot nature of conditional decoding, test-set model selection risk, dependence on target-domain calibration, or possible failure modes of motif vocabularies under distribution shift.

Originality is moderate rather than high: BPE-style token merging is a natural adaptation from NLP and related sequence compression work. The time-series application is useful, but the conceptual novelty is not enough to compensate for the evidential issues.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful idea: adapting byte-pair-style motif tokenization to real-valued time series so that repeated temporal patterns of variable length become discrete tokens. This directly addresses an important inefficiency in sample-wise and fixed-patch tokenization for transformer-based time series models.

The method is technically well motivated and simple enough to be broadly useful. The two-stage quantization plus motif merging procedure is easy to understand, has explicit pseudocode, and gives an adaptive compression mechanism rather than relying on fixed temporal patches.

Conditional decoding is a strong practical contribution. It exploits the discrete vocabulary and continuous values with a closed-form post-hoc estimator, requires no gradient training, has only M^2 parameters, and consistently improves reported MSE, including large gains such as 44.3% on ETTm1 in one setting.

The empirical evaluation is extensive for this type of work. The authors train multiple tokenizer variants and T5 model sizes, compare against Chronos, MOMENT, Morai, and several non-foundation baselines, and evaluate zero-shot forecasting on ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather, Electricity, and Traffic.

The reported efficiency and accuracy gains over Chronos are compelling: average MSE improvements of 36.1% without conditional decoding and 43.2% with conditional decoding, alongside large acceleration factors in several datasets. The analysis of compression, vocabulary complexity, training data size, and learned embeddings adds useful understanding beyond headline metrics.

Presentation is generally strong. The paper clearly separates tokenization, decoding, architecture, and experiments; includes appendix pseudocode and computational cost estimates; and acknowledges limitations such as lack of T5 hyperparameter search and possible benefits from newer architectures.
weaknesses: Some comparisons are not fully controlled. The Chronos comparison is the cleanest, but comparisons with MOMENT and Morai involve different architectures, training strategies, and datasets, which the paper acknowledges. Therefore, the evidence that motifs are superior to patching in general is suggestive rather than definitive.

The conditional decoding experiments partly weaken the claimed zero-shot framing. In the main conditional decoding section, the decoder is trained to dequantize model forecasts on the respective train set and evaluated on the test set, so it uses dataset-specific calibration. This is useful, but should be distinguished more sharply from a purely zero-shot setting.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives pseudocode, hyperparameter references, dataset details, and compute estimates, but it does not clearly commit to releasing code, trained tokenizers, trained models, random seeds, or full tuning protocols. It also states that zero-shot evaluations are run once, so variance and statistical reliability are not established.

The efficiency claims would benefit from more detailed wall-clock accounting. Compression is a meaningful hardware-independent proxy, but the large average acceleration numbers are influenced by dataset/model choices and outliers such as Traffic. More time-to-accuracy results, memory measurements, and tokenizer/decoding overhead analysis would make the efficiency story stronger.

The evaluation covers standard forecasting datasets, but the claim of foundation-model relevance would be stronger with broader coverage, including more diverse domains, longer horizons, multivariate-specific settings, and newer competitive forecasting foundation models or architectures.

The method depends on design choices such as binning distribution, number of bins, minimum motif occurrence, and tokenizer training corpus. The paper ablates these to some extent, but deployment guidance remains limited for practitioners facing data distributions unlike Chronos.

The limitations and ethics discussion is rather brief. The environmental benefit is plausible given compression, but the paper also reports substantial training cost for reproducing the experiments; a more balanced discussion of compute cost, dataset licensing, and possible failure modes under distribution shift would improve the submission.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful idea: adapting BPE-style motif tokenization to time series foundation models, yielding variable-length tokens that can reduce both input length and autoregressive generation steps.

The empirical results are broad and compelling in the main setting: comparisons against Chronos across five datasets and five model sizes show large MSE and inference-time gains, with detailed ablations over quantization granularity, vocabulary size, training data size, robustness, and learned representations.

The method is simple, scalable, and practically appealing. The tokenizer is cheap to train relative to the models, has a fallback to sample-level tokens for unusual patterns, and conditional decoding is analytically fitted with very few parameters.

The presentation is generally strong: the paper clearly separates tokenization, model architecture, conditional decoding, and analysis, and the appendices provide useful details on hyperparameters, compute, variance estimates, and additional experiments.
weaknesses: The strongest zero-shot claims are not fully protected against possible data leakage. The Chronos training corpus is reused for tokenizer/model training, but the paper does not clearly state whether the evaluation datasets or overlapping series are excluded from the Chronos corpus. This is especially important for Electricity, Traffic, Weather, and ETT-style benchmarks.

Conditional decoding is sometimes presented as a universal post-hoc improvement, but the main reported gains fit it on the training split of each evaluation dataset. This makes those results no longer strictly zero-shot and should be separated more clearly from the model- and data-independent conditional decoding setting.

The patch-based baseline is somewhat underexplored. Only a small set of patch lengths is used, the loss/objective differs from the discrete-token models, and stronger or better-tuned patch tokenizers/codebook baselines could reduce the claimed advantage of motifs.

Theoretical claims about linear scaling are underspecified. Vocabulary generation and tokenization by repeated pair replacement can depend on vocabulary size and implementation details, so the asymptotic claim should be stated more carefully despite the reported practical runtime being reasonable.

Main large-scale results are mostly single-run; the variance analysis is limited to small models and a subset of tokenizers. Given the large claimed gains this is not fatal, but stronger uncertainty reporting for the headline comparisons would improve confidence.

The limitations and ethics discussion is quite brief. It mentions lack of hyperparameter search and environmental benefits, but gives little discussion of deployment risks, dataset contamination controls, or the substantial compute required to reproduce all experiments.

strengths: The core idea of applying BPE-style motif vocabularies to discretized time series is interesting and potentially useful. It is simple, computationally plausible, and addresses a real inefficiency in sample-wise tokenization for autoregressive forecasting.

The paper includes a fairly broad empirical study: multiple model sizes, three tokenizer granularities, five datasets, sample-wise and patch-based baselines, ablations on quantization granularity, motif frequency, dataset size, robustness, and embedding analyses.
The method is clearly presented overall, with pseudocode for vocabulary construction/tokenization and useful reporting of inference time, compression ratios, and compute requirements.

The experiments suggest that motif tokenization can improve the quality/efficiency tradeoff relative to a Chronos-style sample-wise tokenizer, especially on Electricity and Traffic, and the adaptive compression behavior is a meaningful practical advantage.
weaknesses: A central claim is overstated: the paper repeatedly frames results with conditional decoding as zero-shot, but the main conditional decoding experiments are trained on the target dataset train split using the model's forecasts and labels. This is supervised target-domain calibration, not zero-shot forecasting, and it accounts for some of the largest reported gains, including the headline 'up to 44%' improvement.

The efficiency and forecasting comparisons are not fully controlled. Motif models receive 128 compressed tokens, which can correspond to substantially more raw historical context than 128 sample tokens for Chronos; thus gains may come from longer effective context, different target compression, and different loss weighting over raw timesteps, not only better tokenization. The paper acknowledges compression but does not disentangle these factors with equal raw-context and equal-token-budget comparisons.

The patch baseline is weakly specified and may be disadvantaged: the authors implement a patch-based Chronos variant with MSE loss rather than comparing to stronger/standard patch foundation-model training choices under matched context, model, and objective. The literature comparison with Moirai/MOMENT is also hard to interpret because architecture and training data differ substantially.

The strongest empirical claims rely on aggregated best-of-many selections across tokenizer choices and model sizes. Selecting the best MSE and separately the fastest model that beats a baseline can inflate the impression of robustness; there is limited statistical testing and most large-scale experiments are run once.

The conditional decoding method is described as universal and no-overhead, but its main form depends on target-domain calibration data and previous-symbol statistics. The more relevant data/model-independent version is relegated to the appendix and shows much smaller and uneven gains, including almost no recovery on Traffic.

The paper's limitations section is too narrow. It mentions lack of hyperparameter tuning and newer architectures, but does not seriously discuss the target-domain calibration issue, context-length confounding, fairness of patch baselines, failure cases such as Weather where motifs hurt without conditional decoding, or the very large compute cost for reproduction.

Reproducibility is incomplete for an ICML main-track claim of this scale. The paper gives hyperparameters and compute estimates, but I did not find a code/model release statement; reproducing the full study requires thousands of H100 GPU hours, and key implementation details such as exact data preprocessing, tokenizer training order, and evaluation/calibration protocol would need to be exceptionally clear.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, original, and useful adaptation of byte-pair-style motif tokenization to time series. The method is easy to understand, has a plausible inductive bias, and directly targets an important bottleneck in transformer-based forecasting: excessive token counts for simple or repetitive sequences.

The empirical evaluation is broad and mostly well structured: the authors train multiple T5/Chronos-scale models, compare against sample-wise Chronos, patch-based Chronos baselines, MOMENT, and Moirai, and report both MSE and inference-time effects across five standard datasets. The reported gains over Chronos are large, especially on Traffic and Electricity.

The paper includes helpful ablations and analyses: quantization granularity, motif occurrence thresholds, tokenizer training-set size, compression variability across datasets and within series, discretization-only baselines, conditional decoding variants, noise/nonstationarity analyses, and embedding-space visualizations.

Reproducibility is better than average for this scale of work: pseudocode, model hyperparameters, data splits, standard deviations for representative settings, profiling details, and compute estimates are provided. The limitations section is honest about the lack of large-scale hyperparameter search.
Conditional decoding is a neat lightweight contribution in its own right. The analytical lookup-table formulation is simple, cheap, and empirically effective for reducing quantization error.
weaknesses: The main zero-shot claims are somewhat overstated when conditional decoding is included. The strongest conditional-decoding results are trained on the target dataset train split and sometimes on model forecasts, which is a form of target-domain calibration even if it uses no gradients. This should be separated more carefully from pure zero-shot evaluation.

Some performance comparisons confound tokenization quality with effective raw-context length. Chronos receives 128 sample tokens, while the motif models receive 128 compressed tokens, corresponding to many more raw time steps depending on compression, especially on highly compressible datasets such as Weather. This is a legitimate advantage of compression, but it weakens claims that forecasting gains are due specifically to better motif representations rather than access to longer histories.

The patch baseline is useful but not fully decisive. The paper modifies Chronos to use continuous non-overlapping patches and MSE, but comparisons to strong patch-based foundation models are less controlled because Moirai/MOMENT differ in architecture, training data, objectives, and context handling. As a result, the conclusion that motifs are generally superior to patching remains suggestive rather than settled.

The evaluation is still concentrated on five standard datasets and a single main forecasting horizon of 64 samples. Given the foundation-model framing, broader coverage over horizons, domains, sampling irregularity, missingness, and multivariate settings would strengthen the generality of the claims.

Reproducibility is limited by scale and missing release details. The appendix estimates many thousands of GPU hours, and I did not see a concrete code/model/tokenizer release plan. The pseudocode is helpful, but independent reproduction of the headline results would be expensive.

The limitations and ethics/impact discussion are brief. The environmental benefit is plausible due to inference compression, but the paper also trains many large models; a more balanced accounting of training cost versus downstream savings would make the sustainability claim more convincing.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful adaptation of BPE-style motif tokenization to time-series foundation models, with a simple mechanism that directly targets both sequence length and temporal-pattern expressivity.

The empirical evaluation is broad: multiple tokenizer granularities, five model sizes, seven zero-shot benchmark settings including Fev-bench, comparisons to sample-wise Chronos, patch-based Chronos variants, and several external foundation models.

The ablation suite is unusually thorough. The manuscript separately studies quantization granularity, motif occurrence thresholds, tokenizer training set size, input length, discretization-only baselines, conditional decoding variants, robustness to noise/trends/outliers, and learned embedding structure.

The reported gains are meaningful: motif tokenization often improves both MSE and inference time, and the authors make a reasonable effort to measure end-to-end runtime including tokenization overhead.
The method is conceptually simple and likely useful in practice, especially for long-horizon or high-throughput forecasting where autoregressive token count matters.
weaknesses: The central novelty is moderate rather than exceptional: BPE over discretized time series is a natural extension of symbolic time-series representations and NLP tokenization. The paper positions it as first pattern-centric tokenization, but related motif/SAX/token-merging literature makes this claim somewhat stronger than warranted.

Some headline numbers are inflated by favorable aggregation choices. Table 2 reports the best MSE and fastest acceleration selected across tokenizers and model sizes, and the very large average speedups depend partly on cases where Chronos is very poor or much larger than the selected motif model.

Conditional decoding is partly a target-domain adaptation method in the main experiments, since it is trained on model forecasts from the respective dataset train split. This is useful, but the paper should more clearly separate zero-shot model performance from supervised post-hoc calibration; the model-independent zero-shot version has much smaller and uneven gains, especially on Traffic.

Comparisons to external foundation models are informative but not fully controlled because backbones, pretraining data, context lengths, probabilistic objectives, and evaluation protocols differ. The paper acknowledges some of this, but conclusions about superiority over patch-based methods should be phrased more carefully.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters, pseudocode, compute, and datasets are described, but no code/checkpoint release is specified, and reproducing the full study requires thousands of H100 GPU hours. Single-run main results with limited seed analysis leave some uncertainty, especially where differences are small.

The limitations and impact discussion are too brief for a paper making large efficiency and sustainability claims. It does not deeply discuss failure modes such as distribution shift outside the quantization range, multivariate dependencies, probabilistic forecasting/calibration, or domains where motif compression may discard rare but important events.

strengths: The core idea of applying BPE-style motif discovery after quantization is simple, relevant, and potentially useful for reducing sequence length in discrete time-series foundation models.

The paper includes a fairly broad empirical study: multiple model sizes, three tokenizer granularities, seven evaluation suites including Fev-bench, comparisons to sample-wise Chronos-style models and several patch-based foundation models, plus ablations on discretization, motif use, input length, vocabulary size, training set size, noise, trends, and outliers.

The method is computationally attractive at inference time, and the authors make a reasonable case that adaptive token lengths can improve both generation speed and forecasting accuracy in some settings.
The presentation is generally clear, with useful pseudocode and readable explanations of the tokenizer and conditional decoding.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are overstated. The abstract and main text repeatedly frame improvements as zero-shot, but the strongest conditional decoding results are trained on the target dataset train split and on model forecasts, making them a form of post-hoc domain adaptation rather than pure zero-shot evaluation.

The headline efficiency numbers are hard to interpret fairly. The reported accelerations come from selecting smaller/faster motif models that beat a chosen Chronos reference, rather than controlled comparisons at matched model size, matched error, matched horizon, and matched context across all baselines.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. Patch-based Chronos is an author implementation with changed loss and limited design exploration, while literature model comparisons mix different backbones, training data, and likely evaluation conventions. The comparison to non-foundation models even uses different context/prediction horizons, which weakens the claim of superiority.

The contribution is incremental in concept: BPE over quantized time-series symbols is a natural adaptation of a known compression/tokenization method. The paper’s novelty rests more on empirical application than on a substantially new algorithmic principle.

Reproducibility is weak for an ICML main-track claim of this scale. The appendix reports thousands of GPU hours, only limited seed replication for small models, and no clear code/model release plan in the manuscript. Many results are single-run and selected across tokenizer/model choices.

The limitations and impact discussion are too thin. They do not seriously address target-dataset calibration, failure modes from quantization outside the bin range, dependence on Chronos data, multivariate structure loss from univariate tokenization, or the cost and accessibility of reproducing the study.

Some analysis claims are suggestive but not decisive. PCA visualizations and correlations between motif length and MSE do not establish that learned tokens capture meaningful causal structure; they mainly show post-hoc associations.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful contribution: adapting BPE-style motif tokenization to time series so that repeated temporal patterns of variable length become discrete tokens. This directly addresses a real bottleneck in sample-wise and fixed-patch time-series transformers: excessive sequence length and rigid compression.

The empirical evaluation is broad and mostly convincing. The authors train multiple T5/Chronos-style foundation models across five sizes and three tokenizer granularities, evaluate zero-shot on seven benchmark collections, and compare against sample-based Chronos, controlled patch-based Chronos baselines, and several recent time-series foundation models. The reported gains are substantial, e.g. average MSE improvements around 40% over Chronos and large inference speedups, with full per-dataset/model results in the appendix.

The experimental design includes several important isolating studies: same-token-budget comparisons, same-input-length comparisons, discretization-only versus motif-token comparisons, patch baselines with similar compression, vocabulary-size and occurrence-threshold ablations, training-set-size studies, and robustness tests for noise, non-stationarity, and transients.

Conditional decoding is a simple but effective post-hoc idea. The paper gives an analytic formulation, studies data/model-dependent and data/model-independent variants, and shows that first-order conditioning captures most of the benefit with very few parameters.

Reproducibility details are better than average for this scale of work: datasets, splits, hyperparameters, seeds for variance estimates, profiling protocol, tokenizer construction cost, and approximate GPU/CPU hours are reported. The paper also honestly acknowledges the lack of large hyperparameter searches due to compute cost.

Presentation is generally strong. The method is easy to understand, the motivation is well connected to current time-series foundation models, and the appendices substantially strengthen the main claims rather than merely adding volume.
weaknesses: The central idea is elegant but conceptually quite direct: quantize the time series and apply BPE-like merging. The originality is useful in this domain, but the paper somewhat overstates novelty with 'first pattern-centric tokenization' given the long history of symbolic time-series representations, motif discovery, SAX-like discretization, and learned discrete patch/codebook approaches. The distinction from these prior lines could be sharpened.

Some of the strongest conditional decoding results are not purely zero-shot: the main data- and model-dependent setting fits decoding parameters on the target train split and evaluates on the target test split. This is a reasonable lightweight adaptation method, but the paper's framing sometimes blends this with zero-shot foundation-model evaluation. The data/model-independent variant helps, but the main headline gains should separate these regimes more clearly.

The evaluation focuses on univariate forecasting with a fixed horizon of 64 samples and MSE. This leaves open how well the tokenizer works for longer horizons, probabilistic forecasting metrics, multivariate dependencies, irregular sampling, missingness beyond a MASK token, and downstream time-series tasks beyond forecasting.

Although the controlled baselines are strong, the comparison to external foundation models is not fully attribution-clean because backbones, pretraining corpora, context lengths, and training objectives differ. The authors acknowledge this, but some conclusions about superiority over patch-based methods should be phrased more cautiously.

Reproducibility is limited by the enormous compute budget: reproducing the model training requires many thousands of H100 GPU hours. The manuscript reports details, but I did not find a concrete code/model/tokenizer release statement, which weakens practical reproducibility for the community.

The limitations section is too short relative to the paper's scope. It mentions lack of hyperparameter search and possible newer backbones, but should also discuss target-domain calibration for conditional decoding, evaluation scope, compute cost, dependence on normalization and quantization range, and possible failure modes when motifs learned from pretraining data poorly match deployment domains.

Some claims are slightly too strong, such as 'adds no computational overhead' for conditional decoding. It may add negligible lookup cost at inference, but it still requires estimating/storing calibration tables and, in the strongest setting, target-domain predictions/labels for fitting.
